questions.question: Which of the following is true about a Super Key?
options: It can never contain more than one attribute
It is always a minimal set of attributes
It uniquely identifies a record in a table
It cannot contain a candidate key
questions.explanation: A Super Key is defined as any set of one or more attributes that can uniquely identify a record in a table, though it is not necessarily minimal.

questions.question: What differentiates a Candidate Key from a Super Key?
options: Candidate Key is a superset of Super Key
Candidate Key contains only numeric values
Candidate Key is a minimal Super Key
Candidate Key can have duplicate values
questions.explanation: A Candidate Key is a minimal Super Key with no unnecessary attributes; removing any attribute breaks uniqueness.

questions.question: How many Primary Keys can a table have?
questions.explanation: A relational table can have only one Primary Key, although it can be composed of multiple columns.

questions.question: Which key is used to reference the primary key of another table?
questions.explanation: A Foreign Key is a column or set of columns in one table that references the primary key (or unique key) in another table.

questions.question: Which of the following keys allows null values and ensures all values are unique?
questions.explanation: A Unique Key constraint ensures all non-null values are distinct and allows NULL values, unlike a Primary Key.

questions.question: A Composite Key is:
options: A key formed from a single column
A key that is derived from a primary key
A key formed from two or more attributes
A foreign key in another table
questions.explanation: A Composite Key is composed of two or more columns that together uniquely identify a record in a table.

questions.question: What is an Alternate Key?
options: A key used when the primary key fails
A candidate key not chosen as primary key
A special type of foreign key
questions.explanation: An Alternate Key is any candidate key that is not selected as the table's primary key; it is also termed a secondary key.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines a Surrogate Key?
options: A composite key derived from candidate keys
A user-generated key used to replace the primary key
A system-generated unique identifier used as a primary key
A natural key used as a foreign key
questions.explanation: A Surrogate Key is an artificial, system-generated unique identifier (such as an auto-increment number or UUID) with no business meaning.

questions.question: A Partial Key is typically used in the context of:
questions.explanation: A Partial Key (or discriminator) is used in weak entity sets to distinguish records within the context of a related strong entity.

questions.question: Which key must have a unique value and cannot be NULL?
questions.explanation: A Primary Key must have strictly unique values for every row and cannot accept NULL values under any circumstance.

questions.question: A table can have:
options: Multiple candidate keys, but one primary key
One primary key and one super key
questions.explanation: A table can have multiple candidate keys, but only one of those candidate keys is chosen to be the primary key.

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about a Foreign Key?
options: It references a primary key in another table
questions.explanation: A Foreign Key does not have to be unique; it can contain duplicate values to establish one-to-many relationships.

questions.question: The key that helps in establishing relationships between two tables is:
questions.explanation: A Foreign Key creates links between tables by referencing the primary or unique key of the parent table.

questions.question: A table has columns A, B, and C. Both (A, B) and (B, C) uniquely identify records. Which are valid composite keys?
questions.explanation: Since both attribute pairs (A, B) and (B, C) can uniquely identify records, both qualify as valid composite keys.

questions.question: Which key is not derived from application data?
questions.explanation: A Surrogate Key is an artificial key generated by the system and is not derived from application or real-world data.

questions.question: In a weak entity set, a partial key is:
options: A key that fully identifies the entity
A key that only partially identifies an entity
questions.explanation: A Partial Key identifies a record only within the subset of an owner entity, requiring the owner's primary key for full identification.

questions.question: A key that includes more attributes than necessary to uniquely identify a record is:
questions.explanation: A Super Key can include extra, unnecessary attributes alongside the identifying attributes while still maintaining uniqueness.

questions.question: Which key(s) can contain null values?
questions.explanation: A Unique Key allows NULL values (depending on DBMS implementation), whereas a Primary Key strictly forbids NULLs.

questions.question: Which of the following is automatically created by the system, typically as an integer or GUID?
questions.explanation: Surrogate keys are generated automatically by database systems, commonly utilizing auto-increment integers or GUIDs/UUIDs.

questions.question: The term "Natural Key" is often used in contrast to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Natural keys (derived from real-world data like email or national ID) are contrasted directly with Surrogate keys (artificial identifiers).

questions.question: Which type of database index is automatically created by default on a Primary Key in most DBMS, compared to a Unique Key?
options: Clustered index for Primary Key, non-clustered index for Unique Key
Non-clustered index for Primary Key, clustered index for Unique Key
Hash index for Primary Key, B-tree index for Unique Key
Bitmap index for Primary Key, clustered index for Unique Key
questions.explanation: In most DBMS implementations, defining a Primary Key automatically creates a clustered index, whereas a Unique Key creates a non-clustered index.

questions.question: Which integrity constraints are enforced by a Primary Key and a Foreign Key, respectively?
questions.explanation: A Primary Key enforces Entity integrity (every record is unique and identifiable), whereas a Foreign Key enforces Referential integrity between tables.

questions.question: How is the composite primary key of a weak entity set formed?
options: By combining the partial key with the primary key of the identifying strong entity
By combining two partial keys from the same weak entity
By combining the partial key with a surrogate key
By assigning a foreign key without any partial key
questions.explanation: A weak entity does not possess a primary key of its own; its primary key is formed by combining its partial key (discriminator) with the primary key of the owner strong entity.

questions.question: In relational database theory, what is the exact relationship between Candidate Keys and Super Keys?
options: Every Super Key is a Candidate Key, but not every Candidate Key is a Super Key
Candidate Keys and Super Keys are completely disjoint sets
A Candidate Key is formed only by combining multiple Super Keys
Every Candidate Key is a Super Key, but not every Super Key is a Candidate Key
questions.explanation: Every Candidate Key is a minimal Super Key, meaning Candidate Keys form a subset of Super Keys, but Super Keys may contain non-minimal extra attributes.

questions.question: An Alternate Key is also referred to as which of the following?
questions.explanation: An Alternate Key is any candidate key not selected as the primary key and is sometimes called a secondary key.

questions.question: In database design, which of the following represents a primary reason to choose a Surrogate Key over a Natural Key?
options: Surrogate keys have rich business logic embedded in their values
Surrogate keys allow multiple NULL values across records
Surrogate keys are always composite keys requiring multiple columns
Surrogate keys remain stable and protect table relationships when real-world natural data changes
questions.explanation: Surrogate keys are chosen because they simplify key management, remain stable over time, and do not change when real-world application data is updated.

questions.question: How do Primary Keys and Unique Keys differ regarding the number of constraints allowed per table?
options: A table can have multiple Primary Keys, but only one Unique Key
A table can have only one Primary Key, but multiple Unique Keys can be defined
Both Primary Keys and Unique Keys are strictly limited to one per table
A table cannot have both a Primary Key and a Unique Key simultaneously
questions.explanation: A relational table is restricted to exactly one Primary Key, whereas multiple Unique Key constraints can be defined on non-primary columns.

questions.question: Under what condition can a Foreign Key column contain NULL values in a relational table?
options: A Foreign Key can contain NULL values if the relationship is optional and NOT NULL is not enforced
A Foreign Key can never contain NULL values under any DBMS
A Foreign Key can contain NULL values only if the referenced Primary Key also contains NULL
A Foreign Key allows NULL values only when used as a composite primary key
questions.explanation: A Foreign Key can contain NULL values to represent optional relationships, provided it has not been explicitly defined with a NOT NULL constraint.

questions.question: When is a database designer most justified in implementing a Composite Key?
options: When referencing a foreign key from a different database instance
When every single column in the table is already completely unique
When the table requires a system-generated auto-increment counter
When no single column is sufficient to guarantee uniqueness, requiring multiple columns together
questions.explanation: A Composite Key is implemented when individual columns contain duplicate values, but their combination guarantees uniqueness for each row.

questions.question: Which of the following combinations of properties strictly defines the requirements for a Primary Key column?
options: Must be unique and must not contain NULL values
Must be unique and must allow one NULL value
Must be minimal and must allow duplicates
Must be system-generated and must be composite
questions.explanation: A Primary Key requires that every value is distinct (Unique) and no value can be missing (NOT NULL).
